tetrahexyldecyl-ascorbate.summary: An oil-soluble vitamin C ester in serums that aims for brighter tone and fewer fine lines, as a gentler alternative to L-ascorbic acid.

quick.overview:
Tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate (THD ascorbate) is a fat-soluble form of vitamin C used in brightening and anti-aging serums. People use it for a brighter, more even tone and softer-looking fine lines, often as a gentler option than L-ascorbic acid, which can be unstable and irritating at high strengths.

Being oil-soluble, it is meant to enter skin and act as an antioxidant and pigment-modulating vitamin C source. Human data come from small, mostly manufacturer-associated studies of multi-ingredient products, including a 2024 randomized double-blind study on facial photoaging. A 2021 lab study found it degrades under oxidative stress unless stabilised, for example with acetyl zingerone.
quick.how: It is applied as a leave-on serum or moisturiser, usually in the morning under sunscreen or in a routine alongside other antioxidants. Formulas often pair it with stabilisers. Brightening and texture changes are typically judged over several weeks of daily use.
quick.risks: Trials of products containing it report generally good tolerance, and no specific serious safety signals turned up. As with any active, mild irritation is possible, and it is a cosmetic ingredient sold without prescription.

angle.text: Tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate is an oil-soluble vitamin C ester used in serums so skin looks brighter and fine lines look softer. It enters skin, works as an antioxidant and pigment modulator, and is chosen as a gentler alternative to L-ascorbic acid. Human data come from small product-level studies.

ethyl-ascorbic-acid.summary: A vitamin C ether sold in brightening serums to even out tone and fade dark marks by slowing melanin production.

quick.overview:
Ethyl ascorbic acid (3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid) is a modified vitamin C used in brightening and anti-aging skincare. People use it to chase an even, radiant complexion and fewer dull or dark patches.

It is described as a tyrosinase inhibitor, the enzyme behind melanin production, so less pigment forms and tone looks more even. Published work is mostly cell studies, animal-skin studies and formulation papers; in cultured cells it reduced melanin production and showed antioxidant effects in UV-exposed keratinocytes. No controlled human trials were found.
quick.how: It is applied as a leave-on serum or cream, commonly in a morning routine with sunscreen, sometimes alongside other brightening ingredients. Tone changes from pigment-targeting products are generally watched over weeks to months.
quick.risks: At least one case report documents allergic contact dermatitis from cosmetics containing it. Systematic safety data are limited. People with reactive skin or known allergies may want to patch test.

angle.text: Ethyl ascorbic acid is a vitamin C derivative used in brightening serums for an even, radiant complexion. It inhibits tyrosinase, which means less melanin and a more even tone. Lab and cell studies support this mechanism.

sodium-ascorbyl-phosphate.summary: A stable, water-soluble vitamin C derivative used for brighter skin and fewer dark acne marks, acting mainly as an antioxidant.

quick.overview:
Sodium ascorbyl phosphate (SAP) is a stabilised, water-soluble form of vitamin C used in cosmetics, mainly as an antioxidant. People use it for brighter tone, fewer dark marks left by acne, and a fresher complexion.

It is meant to convert to vitamin C in skin, where it gives antioxidant protection. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review describes it as functioning primarily as an antioxidant. Most published work covers formulation and stability, including microemulsions and combinations with lipoic acid and vitamins A and E. Registered trials include a 5% SAP lotion for acne and topical antioxidant regimens for photoaging.
quick.how: It is applied as a serum, lotion or cream, often as a steadier alternative to L-ascorbic acid, and used daily. People with acne-prone skin use SAP-based products for marks and breakouts; visible change usually takes several weeks.
quick.risks: A cosmetic safety assessment covers SAP alongside other vitamin C compounds, and no specific harms were found. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient without prescription.

angle.text: Sodium ascorbyl phosphate is a stable vitamin C derivative that people use for brighter skin and fading acne marks. It converts to vitamin C in skin and gives antioxidant protection that supports a more even tone. Formulation data are plentiful, and human appearance trials are fewer.

magnesium-ascorbyl-phosphate.summary: A stable, water-soluble vitamin C derivative in brightening serums for even tone and a fresher look.

quick.overview:
Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate (MAP) is a water-soluble vitamin C derivative used in serums and creams for a brighter, more even complexion and a fresher look. It is promoted as more stable than pure ascorbic acid.

It is described as a pro-drug: it is meant to convert to ascorbic acid after reaching the skin, where it acts as an antioxidant and reduces melanin. Lab work shows ascorbyl esters are more stable than the free acid in formulations, with skin penetration the main challenge. One small study reported improved skin hydration with a MAP product, and reviews note that clinical data on topical vitamin C are limited overall.
quick.how: It is used as a daily serum or cream, often in the morning under sunscreen, and is a common pick for people whose skin dislikes pure ascorbic acid. Brightening is typically judged over weeks of consistent use.
quick.risks: A cosmetic safety assessment covering MAP was published in 2005. It is sold without prescription; labels advise external use and avoiding the eyes.

angle.text: Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate is a stable vitamin C pro-drug used in brightening serums for even tone and a fresher look. It converts to vitamin C in skin, giving antioxidant action and reduced melanin. It is common in products, with few direct human trials.

superoxide-dismutase.summary: An antioxidant enzyme added to anti-aging products to limit oxidative skin damage and slow visible aging.

quick.overview:
Superoxide dismutase (SOD) is a natural enzyme family that neutralises the superoxide radical, and it is added to some creams and oral supplements marketed for antioxidant skin protection. The appearance payoff people want is less oxidative damage and slower visible aging.

SOD converts superoxide into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide; humans have cytosolic (SOD1), mitochondrial (SOD2) and extracellular (SOD3) forms. No published trial of topical SOD for cosmetic anti-aging was found. Registered human trials of SOD concern mostly radiation-related skin injury and oral supplements.
quick.how: It appears as an ingredient in anti-aging creams and serums or as an oral supplement, usually as part of a wider antioxidant routine with sunscreen. Any visible effect is gradual and tied to long-term use.
quick.risks: No cosmetic-specific safety data were found. Bovine-derived SOD drugs were withdrawn in several European countries over prion concerns.

angle.text: Superoxide dismutase is an antioxidant enzyme added to anti-aging products so skin looks younger for longer. It neutralises superoxide radicals, which limits oxidative damage tied to visible aging. It is biologically central, and registered trials concern radiation skin injury and oral supplements rather than cosmetic use.

ubiquinone-topical.summary: Coenzyme Q10 in anti-aging creams, used as an antioxidant for shallower wrinkles and less sun-aged skin.

quick.overview:
Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) is a compound the body makes in mitochondria, and it is added to anti-aging creams for antioxidant effects. People use it hoping for less photoaging damage and shallower wrinkles.

It carries electrons in the mitochondrial chain, and its reduced form acts as an antioxidant. One formulation paper says cosmetic CoQ10 has been reported to reduce photoaging and wrinkle depth, while noting poor bioavailability through skin; delivery systems such as liposomes have been studied to improve uptake. Human trials of topical CoQ10 identified here concern oral and eye conditions rather than wrinkles.
quick.how: It is applied in creams and serums, often with other antioxidants, as part of a daily anti-aging routine. Changes in fine lines are gradual, over months.
quick.risks: Oral CoQ10 is described as generally well tolerated. Topical-specific safety data were not found. It is sold as a cosmetic or supplement and is not an approved anti-aging drug.

angle.text: Topical coenzyme Q10 goes into anti-aging creams as an antioxidant meant to reduce photoaging damage and make wrinkles shallower. One formulation paper reports reduced photoaging and wrinkle depth with cosmetic use, and notes skin penetration is a hurdle. Direct wrinkle trials are scarce.

palmitoyl-tripeptide-1.summary: The collagen-signal peptide half of Matrixyl 3000, used in serums for firmer, smoother skin and fewer wrinkles.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is a lab-made peptide (glycine, histidine and lysine joined to a fatty acid) used in anti-wrinkle creams and serums. People use it for firmer skin and fewer, softer wrinkles. It is one of the two peptides in Matrixyl 3000.

It is described as a signal peptide that prompts skin fibroblasts to make collagen and matrix, and the fatty chain is meant to help it cross the skin barrier. Recent published work is mostly laboratory, permeation and computational studies, and one study found the peptides stayed in the outer layer. No dedicated wrinkle trial was found.
quick.how: It is applied as a daily serum or cream, often in multi-peptide formulas alongside moisturisers and sunscreen. Wrinkle and firmness changes from peptide products are generally assessed over several weeks to months.
quick.risks: It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient. Labels advise external use only, avoiding the eyes and stopping if irritation occurs.

angle.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is a collagen-signal peptide, one half of Matrixyl 3000, used in serums for firmer skin and fewer wrinkles. It signals skin cells to make collagen, which firms the dermis and smooths the surface. Published work is mostly laboratory and permeation studies.

palmitoyl-tetrapeptide-7.summary: The anti-inflammatory peptide half of Matrixyl 3000, used in anti-aging and sensitive-skin products for smoother, calmer skin.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 (sold as Rigin) is a lab-made peptide with a fatty acid tail, used in anti-aging and sensitive-skin products. People use it for smoother, calmer-looking skin. It is paired with palmitoyl tripeptide-1 in Matrixyl 3000.

It is described as an anti-inflammatory signal peptide: in lab models it is reported to reduce IL-6 release, which would mean less inflammation-driven collagen breakdown. Its effects in people have mostly been studied inside multi-ingredient products rather than on its own. Peptides in general are widely used in sensitive-skin products, per an analysis of 88 facial cosmetics.
quick.how: It is used in daily serums and creams, typically in blends with other peptides, and applied to the face and neck. Results from such products are usually judged over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Sold as a cosmetic ingredient; labels advise external use only and avoiding the eyes. No ingredient-specific safety data were found.

angle.text: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 (Rigin) is an anti-inflammatory signal peptide in anti-aging and sensitive-skin products, aimed at smoother, calmer skin. It is reported in lab models to dampen IL-6, limiting inflammation-driven collagen breakdown. Little isolated human data exist.

matrixyl-3000.summary: Sederma's two-peptide blend found in many anti-wrinkle serums, promoted for smoother, firmer skin and fewer visible wrinkles.

quick.overview:
Matrixyl 3000 is a branded peptide complex from Sederma that combines palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7. It is used in anti-wrinkle serums for smoother, firmer, thicker-feeling skin and fewer visible wrinkles.

The peptides are proposed to signal skin cells to repair matrix and to reduce inflammation. Its predecessor, Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4), launched in 2000. A 2026 permeation study detected both peptides in layers of the stratum corneum of three volunteers but they appeared to remain between cells. Independent human data on the blend are limited.
quick.how: It is applied as a daily serum or cream, often in morning and evening routines alongside moisturiser and sunscreen. Wrinkle changes from peptide products are generally assessed over weeks to months.
quick.risks: It is a cosmetic ingredient, and no blend-specific safety data were found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Matrixyl 3000 is a two-peptide blend found in many anti-wrinkle serums, promoted for firmer, smoother skin. The peptides are meant to signal collagen repair and calm inflammation, which firms the skin and softens visible wrinkles. A 2026 permeation study found them in the outer skin layers.

palmitoyl-tripeptide-5.summary: A collagen-signalling cosmetic peptide (Syn-Coll) used in creams, serums and microneedle patches for firmer, smoother skin.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-5, sold as Syn-Coll, is a lab-made peptide attached to a fatty acid and added to anti-wrinkle and skin-firming creams, serums and microneedle patches. People use it for firmer, denser-looking skin and fewer wrinkles.

Suppliers describe it as a signal peptide that stimulates collagen synthesis through a TGF-beta-related pathway, with the fatty chain helping it cross the outer skin layer; this is mainly manufacturer description. Published studies have tested it in multi-ingredient products, such as hyaluronic acid microneedle patches loaded with several peptides, and no standalone placebo-controlled trial was found.
quick.how: It is used as a leave-on serum or cream, or in microneedle patches, often combined with other peptides and hydrating ingredients. Firmness and wrinkle changes are typically assessed over several weeks of daily use.
quick.risks: No specific safety problems are documented in the sources found. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.

angle.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-5 (Syn-Coll) is a collagen-signalling peptide used in creams, serums and microneedle patches for firmer skin and fewer wrinkles. It prompts skin cells to make collagen, which densifies the dermis. Published studies are small and use multi-ingredient products.

palmitoyl-tripeptide-8.summary: A soothing cosmetic peptide (Neutrazen) used to calm irritation and reduce visible redness for a more even-looking face.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-8, sold as Neutrazen, is a lab-made peptide used in products for sensitive, red or irritated skin. People use it to calm irritation and reduce visible redness so the complexion looks more even.

Suppliers describe it as dampening inflammatory signalling in skin, which means less visible redness and discomfort. It has been identified among peptides used in facial products for sensitive skin. Published research is laboratory work or tests of blended formulas, including its use as a targeting molecule for the melanocortin 1 receptor in liposome delivery; no standalone human trial was found.
quick.how: It is applied in leave-on creams and serums made for sensitive or redness-prone skin, usually as part of a gentle daily routine. Calming effects from such products are generally noticed over days to weeks.
quick.risks: Product labels advise a patch test and stopping use if irritation occurs. No specific adverse-effect literature was found.

angle.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-8 (Neutrazen) is a soothing peptide used in products for sensitive or reddish skin, aimed at calmer, more even-looking skin. It is described as dampening skin inflammatory signals, which reduces visible redness. Published research is laboratory and multi-ingredient formula work.

palmitoyl-hexapeptide-12.summary: An elastin-derived cosmetic peptide (Biopeptide EL) in anti-aging creams for firmer, more elastic-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12, sold as Biopeptide EL, is a lab-made peptide based on a repeating elastin sequence and linked to a fatty acid. It is added to anti-aging creams so skin feels firmer and more elastic, with a smoother, younger look.

It is marketed as supporting skin elasticity. A 2025 laboratory study using label-free imaging examined its short-term effects on human skin composition and mechanics, describing it as a self-assembling peptide that interacts with skin components and may alter skin mechanics. No clinical trial results were found.
quick.how: It is used in daily anti-aging creams and serums, often with other peptides and moisturisers. Firmness effects from such products are generally judged over weeks of regular use.
quick.risks: No ingredient-specific harms were found, and safety frameworks for cosmetic peptides are still evolving. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient.

angle.text: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 (Biopeptide EL) is an elastin-derived peptide in anti-aging creams, used for firmer, more elastic skin and a smoother look. It is marketed as supporting skin elasticity. A 2025 imaging study in the lab examined its effects on skin composition and mechanics.

palmitoyl-oligopeptide.summary: A generic ingredient-list term for fatty-acid-linked peptides in anti-aging creams, meant to give firmer, smoother, plumper skin.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl oligopeptide is an ingredient-list term for short peptides attached to palmitic acid, used in anti-aging creams. People use these creams for firmer, smoother, plumper-looking skin.

Formulators describe such peptides as collagen-promoting signal ingredients, with the fatty chain meant to aid skin penetration. Patent literature lists C16 palmitoyl oligopeptides among agents said to promote collagen synthesis. A 2015 methods study used imaging and histology to evaluate the extracellular matrix and epidermal-dermal junction, including effects of age and peptide applications. No dedicated clinical trial was found, and the term covers several different peptides.
quick.how: It shows up on labels of anti-aging creams and serums and is used as part of a daily routine alongside moisturiser and sunscreen. Firmness changes from such products are typically judged over weeks to months.
quick.risks: No specific harms were found in the sources reviewed. It is a cosmetic ingredient; the exact peptide behind the label varies by product.

angle.text: Palmitoyl oligopeptide is a generic label on anti-aging creams for collagen-signalling peptides, used for firmer, smoother, plumper skin. The collagen-promoting claim appears in patent literature. No clinical trial of the ingredient itself was found.

manganese-tripeptide-1.summary: A manganese-bound GHK-style peptide in facial serums for sun damage, dark spots and a more even skin tone.

quick.overview:
Manganese tripeptide-1 is a cosmetic peptide complex used in facial serums for photodamaged skin. It is described as the manganese counterpart of the copper peptide GHK. People use it to address sun damage and dark spots and to even out skin tone.

A single 12-week facial study, in which participants used a serum with the complex twice daily, reported improvement in photodamage signs, especially hyperpigmentation, as judged by participants and a blinded investigator. The study does not establish a mechanism; the ingredient is presented as an analogue of GHK-type peptides. Independent controlled trials have not been identified.
quick.how: It is applied as a facial serum, twice daily in the published study, with changes judged over about 12 weeks. People typically use it alongside sunscreen as part of a routine for pigmentation and photodamage.
quick.risks: The one study reported good tolerability with no significant inflammation. Long-term and comparative safety data have not been published in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Manganese tripeptide-1 is a manganese analogue of GHK used in facial serums for sun damage and dark spots, aiming for clearer, more even skin tone. It targets photodamage and uneven pigmentation. A single 12-week facial study reported improved photodamage signs, most notably pigmentation.

tripeptide-3.summary: A cosmetic peptide marketed for oil control, aimed at less facial shine and a more matte look.

quick.overview:
Tripeptide-3 is a short synthetic peptide used in cosmetics, including products aimed at reducing facial oiliness. People with oily skin look to it for less shine and a more matte face.

Little is published under this name. A 2024 pharmaceutics study developed nanoemulsions to deliver Tripeptide-3 to the skin and reported that, in healthy volunteers over 28 days, the formulation decreased sebum production and increased skin moisture. The study focused on getting the hydrophilic peptide into skin; the abstract does not describe how it affects sebum.
quick.how: It is used in leave-on oil-control serums and lotions applied to the face as part of a daily routine. In the 2024 study, changes were measured over 28 days.
quick.risks: The study included an irritation assessment, though details are limited. No wider safety literature was found.

angle.text: Tripeptide-3 appears in products marketed for oil control, so oily skin looks less shiny and more matte. The aim is lower sebum, which reduces facial oiliness. A 2024 delivery study reported lower sebum and higher moisture in volunteers over 28 days.

tripeptide-10-citrulline.summary: A decorin-mimicking peptide (Decorinyl) meant to organise collagen fibres for firmer, smoother skin.

quick.overview:
Tripeptide-10 citrulline, sold as Decorinyl, is a cosmetic peptide modeled on decorin, a molecule that organises collagen fibres. It is used in anti-wrinkle products for tidier collagen and firmer, smoother skin.

It is designed to bind collagen the way decorin does, regulating fibril diameter and cohesion. In vitro work reported thinner, more uniform collagen fibres. A 24-person randomized study of its combination with acetyl hexapeptide-3 reported measurable changes in skin microtopography and transepidermal water loss. Clinical data are small and mostly in combination.
quick.how: It is used in anti-aging serums and creams, often in combination with other peptides, as part of a daily routine. Texture changes in the small study were measured over a short period of regular use.
quick.risks: The published abstracts do not report adverse effects. Safety data beyond these studies were not found. It is a cosmetic ingredient.

angle.text: Tripeptide-10 citrulline (Decorinyl) mimics decorin to organise collagen fibres, aiming for firmer, smoother skin. In vitro data show more uniform fibres, and one 24-person randomized study of a combination reported changes in skin microtopography.

acetyl-hexapeptide-3.summary: The older name for Argireline, a topical 'Botox-alternative' peptide for softening expression lines around the eyes and forehead.

quick.overview:
Acetyl hexapeptide-3 is the older name of Argireline (acetyl hexapeptide-8), a six-amino-acid cosmetic peptide marketed as a topical alternative to botulinum toxin. People use it to soften expression lines around the eyes and forehead.

It copies a fragment of SNAP-25 and is proposed to interfere with SNARE complex formation, dampening the signals that trigger muscle contraction. Studies suggest it may improve the look of wrinkles, though results are inconsistent and hard to compare, and no dedicated double-blind wrinkle trials were available per Wikipedia. Its large, hydrophilic structure limits skin penetration, which has prompted microneedle and iontophoresis research. It has not been compared directly with botulinum toxin.
quick.how: It is applied as a serum or cream on expression-line areas, commonly the forehead and around the eyes, as part of a daily routine. Wrinkle changes from such products are generally assessed over weeks.
quick.risks: Reported adverse effects in the cited studies were minimal. It is a cosmetic ingredient sold over the counter.

angle.text: Known as Argireline, this peptide is promoted as a topical alternative to Botox for softening expression lines around the eyes and forehead. It is proposed to dampen the signalling that makes expression muscles contract. Human studies on wrinkle depth show modest, inconsistent results.

acetyl-tetrapeptide-15.summary: A soothing peptide (Skinasensyl) for sensitive, reactive skin, aimed at less nerve-driven irritation and calmer-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Acetyl tetrapeptide-15, marketed as Skinasensyl, is a cosmetic peptide for easily irritated skin. People use it so reactive skin looks calmer, with less redness and a more even complexion. It is a minor ingredient, found in about 2 of 88 sensitive-skin products surveyed.

It is described as derived from endomorphin-2 and as acting on mu-opioid receptors to dampen sensory nerve signalling, indirectly reducing TRPV1 responses and CGRP release. Supporting data are a supplier cell study and a 20-person split-face capsaicin test reporting a higher discomfort threshold after four days. A 2021 review found no peer-reviewed publications on it.
quick.how: It is used in leave-on creams and serums for sensitive or reactive skin, applied daily. The supplier study measured effects after four days of use.
quick.risks: No specific adverse events are reported; the review cites supplier safety data. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a medicine.

angle.text: Acetyl tetrapeptide-15 (Skinasensyl) goes into products for sensitive or reactive skin, aiming for calmer, more even-looking skin. It is described as dampening skin nerve signalling to reduce reactivity and redness. Supporting data come from supplier studies, including a 20-person capsaicin test.

acetyl-tetrapeptide-2.summary: A thymopoietin-mimic cosmetic peptide (Thymulen 4) marketed for firmer, younger-looking skin and also found in some hair lotions.

quick.overview:
Acetyl tetrapeptide-2 is a short synthetic peptide (acetyl-Lys-Asp-Val-Tyr) used in skin-firming and anti-aging cosmetics, sold under names such as Thymulen 4, and it appears in some hair lotions. People use it for firmer, tighter, younger-looking skin.

Suppliers say it mimics thymopoietin, a thymus hormone, and prompts keratinocytes to release GM-CSF, activating skin Langerhans cells and supporting epidermal regeneration. A 2018 cell study found it changed stiffness and gene expression (COL17A1) in cultured keratinocytes, and a 2021 randomized study tested a hair lotion combining it with creatine and B vitamins. No trial has tested it alone on facial wrinkles or firmness.
quick.how: It is applied in daily creams and serums for firmness, or in scalp and hair lotions combined with other ingredients. Visible changes from such products are generally judged over weeks to months.
quick.risks: No safety data were found beyond its status as a cosmetic ingredient, and the supporting claims are largely manufacturer-reported.

angle.text: Acetyl tetrapeptide-2 (Thymulen 4) is marketed in skin-firming and anti-aging products to support epidermal regeneration for firmer, tighter skin. Support comes from cell-culture data and one combination-lotion hair study.

acetyl-dipeptide-1-cetyl-ester.summary: A soothing peptide (Calmosensine) for sensitive skin, aimed at less stinging and redness for a calmer complexion.

quick.overview:
Acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester, marketed as Calmosensine, is a peptide derivative used in soothing skincare for sensitive, stinging-prone skin, and it appears in some dermatology-brand soothing creams. People use it for less stinging and redness and a calmer, more comfortable complexion.

It is proposed to increase POMC expression, raising alpha-MSH and beta-endorphin, which lowers CGRP release and so reduces nerve-driven stinging and inflammation. Supplier studies report reduced heat perception and improved comfort. A 2016 split-face capsaicin test in 31 women found no significant effect of a finished product containing it versus a comparator cream, and the review notes the product bases differed. It appeared in about 5.7 percent of 88 sensitive-skin products surveyed.
quick.how: It is used in leave-on soothing creams and serums for reactive skin as part of a gentle daily routine.
quick.risks: No specific adverse events are reported in the review, which cites supplier safety data and CIR assessments. It is a cosmetic ingredient.

angle.text: Acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester (Calmosensine) is used in sensitive-skin products to reduce stinging and redness for a calmer complexion. It is proposed to lower nerve-driven irritation. Supplier data report comfort benefits, while a 2016 capsaicin test of one product found no significant effect.
